top_items.title: Spark-X2.6-4B: The Small 4B Model With a 1M Context Window
top_items.content:
Spark-X2.6-4B is a new 4B open model from the SparkLLM Team, and it scores well above its size on agent and coding tests. It has a 1M-token context window, three thinking levels and an Apache 2.0 licence. It came out a little over a month after Spark-X2.5-4B and uses the same architecture, so the gains come from better post-training. In the video below I test it on real jobs. Here is what it does, how it compares and how to run it.

Key takeaways

- 4B parameters, Apache 2.0, English and Chinese.

- Average benchmark score 63.3 vs 52.1 for Spark-X2.5-4B.

- 1M context, if your device has enough memory.

- Runs in Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM and MLX.

## What is Spark-X2.6-4B?

Spark-X2.6-4B is a small language model from the SparkLLM Team, published on Hugging Face under the XHToken organisation. The model card says it keeps the same architecture as Spark-X2.5-4B, with the improvement coming from post-training. There is also a base checkpoint, Spark-X2.6-4B-Base, if you want to fine-tune it.

Spark-X2.6-4B at a glance

Size
4B parameters, BF16

Layers
36, with 3 sliding-window layers to every 1 full attention layer

Context

Thinking
none, low or high (on by default)

## The 1M context window

The model supports 1,048,576 tokens of context, and the server examples use that full length. The card adds a fair warning: you need enough device memory, so lower the context length if you run out. On long-context tests it does well on Graphwalks 1M (34.2 vs 2.5 for X2.5) but trails Qwen3.5-9B on MRCR v2 at 512K–1M (26.0 vs 34.3).

## Thinking levels

Spark-X2.6-4B has three thinking levels: none, low and high. Thinking is on by default. To turn it off, pass `enable_thinking: false` in the chat template settings. The recommended sampling is temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k -1. Use high for hard maths or coding, and none for quick replies.

## How to run Spark-X2.6-4B

The model card lists all of these:

- Ollama (v0.34.1+): `ollama run SparkLLM/Spark-X2.6-4B`

- LM Studio (0.4.0+): `lms chat spark-x2.6`

- llama.cpp (b10828+): `llama serve -m /path/to/Spark-X2.6-4B-GGUF`

- SGLang: the lmsysorg/sglang Docker image with `--reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser spark25`

- vLLM: with the Spark plugin from GitHub (XHToken/Spark-plugin)

- Transformers: `pip install transformers==4.57.1` and `trust_remote_code=True`

- MLX on Mac: via XHToken/Spark-MLX-LLM

- Fine-tuning: via XHToken/LlamaFactory

It targets NVIDIA GPUs, Ascend NPUs, Apple silicon and Linux CPUs. The card doesn’t give a minimum hardware spec, but a 4B model at 4-bit is small enough for most modern laptops at normal context lengths.

## What I’d use it for

In my video I look at the kind of everyday jobs a small model is good at:

- Onboarding new team members: load your docs and let it answer questions.

- Summarising long documents: the 1M context means you can paste a lot in one go.

- Cheap agent tasks: its tool-calling scores make it a good worker model behind a bigger planner.

- Private work: it runs fully on your own machine.

Be realistic about limits. It is still a 4B model, so for hard reasoning or big code changes, a larger model will do better. Two of the in-house benchmarks, SWebBench and PAgentBench, are not public yet; the team says they will be open-sourced soon.

Want a shorter take? I also cover Spark-X2.6-4B on the AI Profit Boardroom blog.

The architecture is the same, so everything you learned with Spark-X2.5-4B carries over. The difference is post-training, and the jump is large for a release that came only a little over a month later:

## Who is Spark-X2.6-4B for?

It is a good fit if you want an AI model that runs on your own laptop, costs nothing per message and keeps your data private. Small business owners can use it to answer team questions from a handbook, sum up long reports or sort incoming messages. Developers can use it as a cheap worker model inside an agent, where a larger model plans and Spark carries out the tool calls.

It is not the right pick if you need the very best answers on hard reasoning or large code changes. For that, a bigger model will still do better. The smart move is to try Spark on your simplest daily jobs first, see how far it gets, then decide which tasks to hand to it for good.

## How to get good results from a small model

- Give it one clear job at a time instead of a long list of tasks.

- Use high thinking for maths, code and multi-step tool use, and none for quick chat.

- Pair it with a bigger planner. Let a large model plan and Spark do the cheap tool calls.

- Watch your memory at long contexts. Start at 32K–128K and only go higher when you need it.

- Test it on your own data, because benchmarks are only a guide.

Used like this, a 4B model can handle a surprising amount of daily work for close to zero cost.

## My verdict on Spark-X2.6-4B

For a 4B model, the agent and coding scores are very strong, and it is easy to run in Ollama or LM Studio. If you want a small, private, free model for summaries, tool calls and support tasks, Spark-X2.6-4B is one of the best small models to try right now.

### Who made Spark-X2.6-4B?

The SparkLLM Team, which publishes its models on Hugging Face under the XHToken organisation.

### What is Spark-X2.6-4B’s context window?

Up to 1,048,576 tokens (1M), as long as your device has enough memory.

### How do I run Spark-X2.6-4B in Ollama?

Use Ollama v0.34.1 or later and run: ollama run SparkLLM/Spark-X2.6-4B.

### Is Spark-X2.6-4B better than Qwen3.5-9B?

On the model card’s average it scores 63.3 vs 49.1, and it leads on tool calls, browsing and SWE-bench. Qwen3.5-9B still wins on GPQA Diamond and some long-context tests.

### Can I turn off thinking?

Yes. It has none, low and high levels. Pass enable_thinking false in the chat template settings to turn thinking off.

Hermes Agent Step 5 means running StepFun’s new Step 5 Preview model as the brain of Hermes Agent. In the video below I connect it to Hermes and use it for research, drafting, voice and chained agents. Here is how to set it up, what it costs and how it compares.

Key takeaways

- Official pricing: $1.00 input and $2.70 output per million tokens.

- Connect it with the stepfun provider or through Nous Portal.

- Open weights with a StepFun licence that adds conditions for very large companies.

## What is Step 5 Preview?

Step 5 Preview comes from StepFun. The Hugging Face model card calls it “StepFun’s flagship model for agentic work”. It is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 600B total parameters and 27B active per token, and it takes text and images as input.

Those API limits come from the StepFun docs.

## Is Step 5 free in Hermes?

I want to be clear here. In my video it was free to run inside Hermes at the time of recording. Check current pricing before you rely on that. I couldn’t find an official source that confirms a free window, which provider offers it or when it ends.

The official numbers are these. StepFun’s pricing page lists step-5-preview at $1.00 per million input tokens ($0.10 on a cache hit) and $2.70 per million output tokens. The Nous inference API listed stepfun/step-5-preview at the same paid price when we checked, with no free variant at that time.

Free windows change fast. Before you build a workflow around Step 5, open Hermes’s model picker and check the price shown for the model you pick.

## How to set up Step 5 in Hermes Agent

From the Hermes docs, there are two ways.

### Option 1: StepFun API key

- Get an API key from StepFun.

- Add `STEPFUN_API_KEY=your-key` to `~/.hermes/.env`.

- The default base URL is `https://api.stepfun.com/v1`. Use `STEPFUN_BASE_URL` to change it.

- Start a chat: `hermes chat --provider stepfun --model step-5-preview`.

- To make it your default, set `model.provider` and `model.default` in config.yaml.

### Option 2: Nous Portal

Run `hermes chat --provider nous` or use `hermes model` to open the model picker, then choose Step 5 Preview. This route bills through your Nous account.

In the video I put the combo through everyday agent jobs:

- Taught Hermes a new skill in seconds. Hermes’s skill_manage tool writes the skill for you.

- Research and drafting with live web search.

- Talked to it out loud with voice mode: `/voice on`, then Ctrl+B to record.

- Shared memory through my Obsidian vault.

- Chained agents, one handing work to the next.

## The licence: what you need to know

The weights are open under the StepFun Model License 1.0, which StepFun describes as Apache-2.0-style with attribution and some commercial conditions. If your product has over 100M monthly active users or over $20M revenue a month, you must show “Powered by StepFun AI”. Device makers and model-as-a-service businesses with over $20M revenue over 12 months need a separate commercial licence. Internal use is exempt. For almost every small business, it works like a normal open licence.

## Running it yourself

You can self-host the weights with vLLM or SGLang (OpenAI-compatible) or Transformers. It is big: the FP8 build needs a 4×B300 node or an 8×H200 node. Recommended settings are temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 0. For most people the API route is far easier.

## Tips for using Step 5 in Hermes

- Pick the effort level. Use low for quick replies and high for research and coding.

- Start a new session at task boundaries with /new, so the model works from a clean context.

- Turn repeated jobs into skills, so you don’t paste the same instructions every day.

- Watch your spend. At $2.70 per million output tokens, long agent chains add up, so check usage after your first few runs.

Step 5’s 1M context is handy for long research jobs, but large prompts still cost money. Keep only what the task needs in the conversation.

Step 5 Preview is a capable, fairly cheap agent model, and it plugs into Hermes with one provider setting. Use the free window if it is still open when you read this, but plan around the official $1.00/$2.70 pricing.
